views.caveat: Many in this strand reject framing the vacanas' Lord in Vedāntic or Sanskrit-philosophical terms.

descriptions: the divine as the Mother of all, served in the sick and the outcaste
views.relation_to_self: The same Aghora teaching of non-difference, turned toward service.
views.relation_to_world: The world is served, not shunned.
views.caveat: Recent movement; formulation from general reports, not from its own texts.

descriptions: the true name of the formless Lord
negations: no image
views.relation_to_self: The true name within.
views.relation_to_world: All castes equal before him.
views.caveat: Three distinct movements; characterization low confidence.

names.name: Civam (as the source of the medical knowledge)

descriptions: Siddha medicine places itself within the Siddhars' Śaiva frame: Śiva is the first teacher of medicine; body and cosmos share the five elements and the ninety-six principles.
views.relation_to_self: The soul inhabits a body of 96 principles whose health is the balance of the three humours.
views.relation_to_world: The body is built of the five elements, like the world; macrocosm and microcosm correspond.
views.caveat: A medical system: it does not itself argue a doctrine of the ultimate, but borrows the Siddha/Śaiva frame; practitioners hold a range of religious views.

names.name: Paramākāśa / dahara (the supreme ether in the heart)

descriptions: Śiva endowed with cit-śakti, free from all defects, the material and efficient cause of the world.
The supreme ether of the Upaniṣads is his śakti; he is to be meditated on in the small space of the heart.
negations: Denies an attributeless Brahman without śakti.
Denies that Śiva is only the efficient cause.
views.relation_to_self: Souls (paśu) are his body and attribute, distinct yet inseparable; liberated, they become equal to Śiva in bliss (śiva-sāmya) but not identical.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real, a manifestation of the subtle world held in Śiva's śakti.
views.caveat: Appayya Dīkṣita read the school as a step towards Advaita; the school's own text and its Vīraśaiva heirs hold the qualified non-dualism as final.

descriptions: that in which all this rests and from which it has come forth; its nature is unobstructed (Spandakārikā 1.2)
the inner (antarmukha) agency, seat of omniscience, never lost (SK 1.14-16)
the opening and closing of Śaṅkara's eyes (SK 1.1)
negations: where there is neither pain nor pleasure, neither object nor subject, nor even insentience - that exists in the supreme sense (SK 1.5)
views.relation_to_self: It is one's own nature (svabhāva), the knower-agent persisting through all states (SK 1.3, 1.10).
views.relation_to_world: The world emerges and dissolves with the unmeṣa and nimeṣa of the one Śaṅkara (SK 1.1); all particular vibrations rest on the universal vibration (SK 1.19).
views.caveat: Spanda insists that the ultimate is dynamic; it would reject any account of a static, inactive absolute.

descriptions: Tripurā is the supreme, whose nature is the fusion (sāmarasya) of light (prakāśa) and self-awareness (vimarśa) (Amṛtānanda on Yoginīhṛdaya 1.6).

Maheśa, whose body is pure light, holds self-awareness within; the primal Śakti is the stainless mirror in which Śiva knows himself; their union is the great point (mahābindu) and the 'I' (Kāmakalāvilāsa 1-5).
She is consciousness-power (citśakti) and also the power of the insentient (Lalitā Sahasranāma 90).
She is 'the form of the oneness of Śiva and Śakti' and dwells in the king of cakras (Lalitā Sahasranāma 182-183).
When the supreme Śakti, by her own will, beholds her own vibrancy, the cakra (the universe) arises (Yoginīhṛdaya 1.9-10).
negations: nirguṇā, niṣkalā, nirupādhi — beyond qualities, parts and limiting adjuncts (Lalitā Sahasranāma 43-45)
beyond the reach of mind and speech (manovācām agocarā, Lalitā Sahasranāma 89)
views.relation_to_self: The Goddess is one's own self: the jīva is Śiva clothed in coverings, Paraśiva is the uncovered (PKS 1.5); worship is the contemplation of the non-difference of knower, knowing and known (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
views.relation_to_world: The universe of thirty-six principles is the Śrīcakra, her self-expansion; she herself becomes mind, space, air, fire, water and earth, and nothing lies beyond her (Saundaryalaharī 35).
views.caveat: Śrīvidyā holds that the Goddess in union with Śiva is the one ultimate, and treats the one-truth principle as its own (she is worshipped by all the gods). It would reject a reading that makes Lalitā one symbol among equals or that denies the reality of her power. Within the tradition the Samaya school insists on the strict equality of Śiva and Śakti, while uttara-Kaula readings hold Śakti alone; Bhāskararāya's gloss 'substratum of the false world' (name 735) leans to Advaita, while the Kāmakalāvilāsa speaks of real manifestation — these differences are recorded, not erased.

descriptions: the coolness of the extinction of defilements, available here and now, momentarily (tadaṅga-nibbāna) and finally
the mind void of 'I' and 'mine' (chit wang)
views.relation_to_self: nibbāna is the complete absence of the illusion of 'I' and 'mine'
views.relation_to_world: not a place or a heaven after death; found in the midst of life
views.caveat: Buddhadāsa described Dhamma, God and nature in parallel terms in dialogue with other religions, but denied a personal creator; the one-truth reading is a reconciliation he partly invited.

descriptions: reached by unbroken mindfulness of touch and feeling when sensation, including pain, is penetrated and ends
views.caveat: The Sunlun teaching speaks little about the ultimate in abstract terms; entry kept minimal.

names.name: the Lord of the Dance (Naṭarājaṉ, Ampalavāṇaṉ)

descriptions: the Real (cat), known neither as a sense-object nor as nothing, but by grace
pervades all as the vowel 'a' pervades letters (Tiruvaruṭpayaṉ 1.1)
of eight qualities (eṇkuṇam)
grace (aruḷ) is his power, and he comes as the guru
dances the five acts at Chidambaram
negations: not the object of the senses (Civañāṉa Pōtam 6)
not one with souls in substance; not two in separation
views.relation_to_self: Advaita as inseparability: one with, other than, and together with souls; the freed soul abides in him enjoying his bliss.
views.relation_to_world: Efficient cause of the real world produced from māyā; the world is 'acat' only as perishing, not as illusion.
views.caveat: The Tamil school calls its view non-dual but insists on three eternal realities; it rejects Advaita's identity and unreality of the world.

descriptions: self-luminous everywhere, dwelling in the heart of those who love (Kaṭuveḷi 34)
love itself is Civam (TM 270)
the undivided fullness beyond qualities (Rāmatēvar 1)
light within like the inner light of a ruby (Aḻukaṇṇi 39)
without here or there, everywhere as light, fullness of bliss, filled with grace (Tāyumāṉavar)
negations: not the planted stone (Sivavākkiyar)
not seen by the four Vedas (Pattirakiriyār 48)
not reached by pilgrimage or holy bathing (Kaṭuveḷi 15)
beyond elements, senses, qualities and instruments (Paṭṭiṉattār, Tiruvēkampamālai 31)
views.relation_to_self: Within the body and the heart; the seeker longs to stand as 'I am He' (Pattirakiriyār 219) and asks 'who am I, who are you'; guru and Lord are one; devotional and non-dual voices coexist.
views.relation_to_world: The world and body are real enough to be perfected (TM 724–725) yet impermanent, a bubble and a leaking pot; macrocosm and microcosm mirror each other.
views.caveat: The Siddhars are not one school: some speak as Śaiva devotees, some as non-dualists of the void, some as alchemists of the deathless body. They would reject any reading that places the ultimate in a temple image or makes caste or scripture a condition of reaching it.

descriptions: as in Viśiṣṭādvaita generally; with the emphasis that the Lord himself is the already-accomplished means (siddhopāya) whose grace is causeless, who relishes even his devotees' faults, and to whom Śrī, ever inseparable, mediates
negations: as for Viśiṣṭādvaita
views.relation_to_self: The soul's essence is to belong wholly to the Lord (ananyārha-śeṣatva) and to be dependent (pāratantrya); it brings nothing of its own to its salvation.
views.relation_to_world: As for Viśiṣṭādvaita: the world is the real body of the Lord.
views.caveat: Same caveat as ult:visistadvaita; in addition the Teṅkalai reject any view that the soul's own act contributes to its salvation.

descriptions: the heart released from all defilements, known directly by the one who has reached it
Ajahn Maha Boowa: the 'pure citta' after even the radiant point of the mind — the seat of ignorance — has been destroyed; it does not die
Ajahn Chah: the unconditioned is realized by letting go; 'peace' beyond happiness and suffering
views.relation_to_self: the teachers deny that the released heart is a self, yet speak of it in positive terms (pure, deathless), a feature noted by other traditions
views.relation_to_world: beyond the conventions (sammuti) of the world, while conventions are still used
views.caveat: The forest teachers would reject a reading of the released citta as an ātman or a cosmic self; they speak from their practice, not as metaphysics.

names.name: paramattha-dhamma nibbāna (the fourth ultimate reality, beside citta, cetasika and rūpa)

descriptions: the one unconditioned dhamma, outside the five aggregates and the three periods of time; object of the path and fruition consciousness
one in nature (santi-lakkhaṇa, the characteristic of peace) but described as with residue (sa-upādisesa, the arahant's living) and without residue (anupādisesa, at the arahant's death) (Iti 44)
described by the commentaries as existing (atthi) and not mere non-existence, against those who say it is only the absence of the defilements
negations: not a self (sabbe dhammā anattā — Dhp 279, read by the commentaries to include nibbāna)
not produced by the path but realised by it; without arising, change or passing away (AN 3.47)
views.relation_to_self: Nibbāna is anattā; there is no self that attains it — 'suffering exists, but no sufferer; nibbāna exists, but no one who is extinguished' (Visuddhimagga 16.90, a commentarial verse; see U37).
views.relation_to_world: The unconditioned is distinct from the conditioned world (saṅkhata) and is not its cause; the world is dependently arisen.
views.caveat: Theravāda affirms nibbāna as a real, single unconditioned dhamma but explicitly rejects that it is a self, a soul-substance, a creator or a cosmic ground; it would reject the identification of nibbāna with Brahman or ātman made in some reconciliations (the Kathāvatthu and the commentaries argue against any permanent self).
views.notes: The commentarial and Abhidhamma details are skeleton pointers; U37 owns the Abhidhamma and Visuddhimagga.

descriptions: the Heart of Bhairava, in which the whole moving and unmoving world rests as the great tree rests in the banyan seed (Parātrīśikā 24)
Bhairava's state, indescribable, full (bharita), identical with the supreme Goddess (Vijñāna Bhairava 14-18)
the one consciousness whose powers are Parā, Parāparā and Aparā (will, knowledge, action; TĀ 1.271-272)
negations: the forms of Bhairava with parts (sakala) are for meditation of the confused; in truth he is not these (VBT 8-13)
views.relation_to_self: The limited individual (nara/aṇu) is Śiva through Śakti; śakti is the door into Śiva (VBT 20-21).
views.relation_to_world: The world is the unfolding of the Heart through the letters (mātṛkā) and the tattvas; it is within Bhairava as his power.
views.caveat: The Trika insists on the triadic self-unfolding of the one and on its own superiority to other revelations.

descriptions: the ultimate truth beyond mind and matter, experienced when the arising and passing of sensations is fully penetrated and all saṅkhāras are eradicated
described in courses as the stage beyond the field of mind and matter, where nothing arises
views.relation_to_self: the 'I' is a mass of vibrations arising and passing; no permanent self
views.relation_to_world: the world of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa) is experienced as constantly arising and passing; nibbāna is beyond it
views.caveat: Presented as a universal law of nature (dhamma) rather than as a theology; the tradition would reject speculation about the ultimate in place of practice.

descriptions: The the eight Uḍupi maṭhas holds the Dvaita teaching on the ultimate without variation; see ult:dvaita.
views.relation_to_self: As in ult:dvaita.
views.relation_to_world: As in ult:dvaita.
views.caveat: As in ult:dvaita; the maṭha has no separate doctrine of the ultimate.

descriptions: satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma — truth, knowledge, infinite (TU 2.1.1)
sad eva ... ekam evādvitīyam — being alone, one without a second (ChU 6.2.1)
vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma — understanding, bliss (BAU 3.9.28); raso vai saḥ (TU 2.7.1)
that from which beings are born, by which they live, into which they enter (TU 3.1.1)
sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma — all this is brahman (ChU 3.14.1); brahmaivedaṃ viśvam (MuU 2.2.11)
pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam — that is full, this is full (BAU 5.1.1)
the Lord who wields māyā, whose power is innate knowledge and strength (ŚU 4.10, 6.8)
negations: asthūlam anaṇu ... — not gross, not fine ... without inside or outside (BAU 3.8.8)
aśabdam asparśam arūpam avyayam (KU 1.3.15); adreśyam agrāhyam (MuU 1.1.6)
yato vāco nivartante — from which words turn back with the mind (TU 2.4.1)
nāntaḥprajñaṃ na bahiṣprajñaṃ ... the fourth (MāU 7)
known by the one to whom it is unknown (Kena 2.3)
views.relation_to_self: The self is declared to be brahman (ahaṃ brahmāsmi, tat tvam asi, ayam ātmā brahma, prajñānaṃ brahma); it is also the inner controller of every being (BAU 3.7) and, in the two-birds image, the Lord beside the grieving self (MuU 3.1.1-2; ŚU 4.6-7).
views.relation_to_world: The source, support and end of all beings (TU 3.1.1); the world is woven on the imperishable (BAU 3.8) and pervaded by the Lord (Īśa 1); it emanates like sparks from fire (BAU 2.1.20; MuU 2.1.1), becomes manifest by name and form (BAU 1.4.7; ChU 6.3.2), and its modifications are 'a verbal handle, a name' (ChU 6.1.4); in the ŚU the māyin projects it by māyā-prakṛti (4.9-10).
views.caveat: The Upaniṣads do not systematize; they state identity (the mahāvākyas), difference (the two birds; the inner controller 'other than' what it controls) and a personal Lord (Śvetāśvatara). The later Vedānta schools read these same texts in very different ways — see dsp:tat-tvam-asi, dsp:souls-one-or-distinct, dsp:world-real-or-appearance, dsp:saguna-nirguna and dsp:being-or-non-being-first; this view records the statements without deciding between those readings.

descriptions: The Uttarādi Maṭha holds the Dvaita teaching on the ultimate without variation; see ult:dvaita.
views.relation_to_self: As in ult:dvaita.
views.relation_to_world: As in ult:dvaita.
views.caveat: As in ult:dvaita; the maṭha has no separate doctrine of the ultimate.

names.name: Śrīman Nārāyaṇa (the divine couple, Śrī and Nārāyaṇa)

descriptions: as in Viśiṣṭādvaita generally; with the emphasis that Śrī, all-pervading like Viṣṇu, shares his supremacy and is, with him, the means and the goal (the divine pair, mithuna, is the object of surrender)
negations: as for Viśiṣṭādvaita
views.relation_to_self: The soul is the servant of the divine couple; it must, by the Lord's grace, perform surrender as the means.
views.relation_to_world: As for Viśiṣṭādvaita: the world is the real body of the Lord.
views.caveat: Same caveat as ult:visistadvaita; in addition the Vaṭakalai insist that Śrī is not of the rank of souls.

names.name: the five forms: Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Aniruddha

descriptions: Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman, the highest Self; his highest form is subtle, imperishable and partless (niṣkala); his gross form with parts (sakala) is the cause of all (Kriyādhikāra 11.148–150).
views.relation_to_self: The worshipper attains Viṣṇu's world and nearness to him in graded forms of liberation (sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya).
views.relation_to_world: Nārāyaṇa is the cause of the whole world; Vikhanas, author of the Sūtra, is born of him (Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa).
views.caveat: The Vaikhānasas insist on the Vedic identity of their worship and would reject being classed with tantric Āgama theologies.

descriptions: Saluted as 'Īśvara, the cause' at the opening of the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha; the knowledge that leads to the highest good arises from dharma manifested by His command.
By His will the world is dissolved at the end of a Brahmā's lifespan and created again for the selves' experience, through their adṛṣṭa (Praśastapāda).
The highest good (niḥśreyasa) is the fruit of dharma (VS 1.1.2): liberation, in which the self has no contact with a body (VS 5.2.20).
negations: the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra itself does not name Īśvara
views.relation_to_self: The Lord is a self distinct from the innumerable individual selves, each made distinct by its own ultimate particularity (viśeṣa).
views.relation_to_world: Efficient cause who initiates the motion of eternal atoms at creation and their separation at dissolution; the nine substances and the other categories are real.
views.caveat: Early Vaiśeṣika (the sūtras) does not explicitly name a Lord (scholarly account); theism appears from Praśastapāda on. The school would reject monism: innumerable eternal atoms, selves and minds, each individuated by ultimate particularity, are irreducibly many — the school's very name is traditionally linked with 'particularity'.

descriptions: the truth of man, above which there is nothing
the union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa within the human pair
negations: not known by the one who has not crossed the darkness
views.relation_to_self: Every person's true form (svarūpa) is Kṛṣṇa or Rādhā.
views.relation_to_world: The eternal Vṛndāvana is within the body.
views.caveat: Orthodox Gauḍīyas reject the identification of human partners with Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa; the Sahajiyā rejects the orthodox reading as merely outward.

names.name: the Self known by itself (svasaṃvedya ātmarūpa)

descriptions: the Primal One set forth by the Vedas, known by itself, whose form is the Self (Jñāneśvarī 1.1)
the one reality that appears as Śiva and Śakti and sports as the world (Amṛtānubhava)
the beautiful form standing on the brick, hands on hips, mother to the devotee
smaller than an atom and vast as the sky (Tukārām)
negations: not described by sat, cit or ānanda, which only exclude their opposites (Amṛtānubhava 5)
not reached by the word, which ends before the self-evident (Amṛtānubhava 6)
views.relation_to_self: The Self is the Lord; yet devotion continues after knowledge — God worships God.
views.relation_to_world: The world is the play of the one consciousness, not a second thing; seen through the saints it is the Lord's (onion and radish are Viṭṭhala).
views.caveat: The Vārkarīs hold the personal Viṭṭhala and the non-dual Self together; they would reject a reading that makes the form merely provisional for beginners.

names.name: the one self (eka ātman) of the deity, praised in many ways
the great god (mahān devaḥ) who is speech, entering mortals
the imperishable (akṣara), reached by the higher knowledge

descriptions: Because of the deity's great majesty the one self is praised in many ways; the other gods are its limbs (Nirukta 7.4).
The deities are three by station yet may be taken as person-like, not person-like, or both (Nirukta 7.5–7).
Grammar is studied so that we may become equal to the great god, speech (Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā).
The Vedas and their six limbs are the lower knowledge; the higher is that by which the imperishable is attained (MuU 1.1.4–5).
views.relation_to_self: The seers saw the hymns when Brahman came upon them (Nirukta 2.11); some hymns speak in the first person of the self (ādhyātmika, Nirukta 7.1).
views.relation_to_world: The gods and their powers are the limbs and functions of one self; time, the year and its cycle are presided over by Prajāpati (VJ Ṛk 1).
views.caveat: The Vedāṅgas describe themselves as lower knowledge and posit no systematic doctrine of the ultimate; the grammarians' śabda-brahman belongs to lin:vyakarana (U31). They would not accept a one-truth reading that loosens the exact letter, accent and sequence of the Veda, which must be preserved as it is.

descriptions: that from which the origin, sustenance and dissolution of this world proceed (BS 1.1.2)
known from scripture (BS 1.1.3), the purport of all Upaniṣadic texts (BS 1.1.4)
conscious: it 'thought' before creating (BS 1.1.5)
material and efficient cause of the world (BS 1.4.23)
creates as sport (līlā), without need (BS 2.1.33)
the goal attained by the liberated, from which there is no return (BS 4.4.22)
negations: the 'not so, not so' denies 'so much' (the two forms) of Brahman (BS 3.2.22)
not distinguished by place/limiting adjuncts (BS 3.2.11)
views.relation_to_self: Debated within the sūtras themselves: Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi and Kāśakṛtsna give three accounts (BS 1.4.20–22); every Vedānta school reads the sūtras on this point differently.
views.relation_to_world: Brahman is the world's cause; the effect is non-different from the cause (BS 2.1.14); the manner (real or apparent transformation) is the chief point of divergence among commentators.
views.caveat: This view records what the sūtras state on their face. Each Vedānta school's reading (Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, Bhedābheda etc.) is its own view, and the schools deny that the others' readings are the sūtras' meaning.

descriptions: The One Being that the inspired call by many names — Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, Yama, Mātariśvan (RV 1.164.46); the one bird the poets shape into many (10.114.5); the One that has become all this (8.58.2).
That One which breathed windless by its own power before there was being or non-being, death or immortality, and was born by the power of tapas (RV 10.129.2–3).
The Person who is all this, what was and what will be, lord of immortality; one quarter of him is all beings, three quarters the immortal in heaven (RV 10.90.2–3).

The highest Brahman whose alone is the light; those who know Brahman in man know the Supreme (AVŚ 10.8.1, 10.7.17); the one-alone god in whom the gods become one (AVŚ 13.4.12–13); 'that is Agni, that the Sun … that is brahman' (VS 32.1).
The self, desireless, wise, immortal, self-existent, lacking nothing; knowing him one does not fear death (AVŚ 10.8.44).
negations: 'Then there was neither non-being nor being' (RV 10.129.1)
'Who really knows? … perhaps he does not know' (RV 10.129.6–7)
'There is no likeness of him' (VS 32.3)
'You will not find him who produced these — something else has come between you' (RV 10.82.7)
'He is called neither second nor third …' (AVŚ 13.4.16–18)
views.relation_to_self: Named in the Saṃhitās as the self of what moves and stands (Sūrya, RV 1.115.1), the self present in the golden city of the body (AVŚ 10.2.32–33), the one god who entered the mind (AVŚ 10.8.28) and the ageless self known by the wise (10.8.44); the seer who first 'does not know what he is' (RV 1.164.37) can also say 'I was Manu and the Sun' (4.26.1).
views.relation_to_world: Both immanent and exceeding: the One has become all this (RV 8.58.2) and the Person covers the earth and exceeds it by ten fingers, three quarters of him beyond (10.90.1–3); the world is made by sacrifice of the Person, by the All-maker, from the Golden Germ, by tapas, or from Time — accounts the Saṃhitās place side by side.
views.caveat: The Saṃhitās are a liturgy addressed to many gods, each praised in turn as supreme; the statements of one ultimate are a minority of speculative hymns, and they leave the origin itself in question (10.129.6–7). The ritual tradition's own hermeneutics (Mīmāṃsā) reads the corpus for injunctions and holds the deities to be what the mantras name, positing no single describable ultimate; Yāska records the view that there are three deities (Nirukta 7.5) beside the view that one Self is praised in many ways (7.4); Vaiṣṇava readers take the One as Viṣṇu. The one-truth reading (RV 1.164.46) is used by this ontology only in the interpretation layer.

descriptions: The supreme is Bhairava in union with his power(s); in later Vidyāpīṭha texts the goddess becomes primary.
views.caveat: Catalogue-level summary; the doctrinal views of the Trika and Kālīkula are recorded by U19/U24.

descriptions: the liṅga in which the world dissolves and from which it arises; being-consciousness-bliss (SSM 6.36–38)
the pedestal is Śakti, the liṅga Paraśiva, the universe their union (SSM 11.32)
the liṅga of light shining in all beings (SSM 6.35)
the ocean of consciousness whose waves are the thirty-six tattvas (SSM 1.3)
the one god among the many household gods (Basava)
the husband who does not die or decay (Akka Mahādēvi)
negations: beyond contemplation and unmanifest (SSM 6.51)
where neither sun nor moon shines (SSM 12.38)
not the avyakta with Maheśvara as its bearer (SSM 12.37)
the void, bayalu (Allama)
views.relation_to_self: The soul (aṅga) is a part of Śiva through beginningless ignorance and progresses through six stations to union (aikya, sāmarasya); in practice the relation is master and servant, and at union difference is seen to be imagined by māyā.
views.relation_to_world: The world arises from Śiva and is not different from him, as his Śakti's manifestation and his body (aṣṭamūrti) — neither identical with nor separate from him; for the śaraṇas the moving devotee is his living temple.
views.caveat: The tradition speaks with two voices: the Pañcācārya strand calls its doctrine Śivādvaita or Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita and insists that difference is real at the level of practice; the vacana strand names Śiva as a personal lord and as the void and resists Vedāntic framing. Both would reject a reading of the one truth that makes the world, the liṅga or devotion illusory (SSM 10.37–43).

descriptions: the one Brahman qualified by sentient and insentient beings as its body (cid-acid-viśiṣṭa)
opposed to all that is evil (akhila-heya-pratyanīka) and the sole abode of infinite auspicious qualities (kalyāṇaika-tāna) — the twofold mark (ubhaya-liṅga)
satyam jñānam anantam: real, knowledge, infinite — each word naming a quality of one Brahman, not an attributeless essence
material and efficient cause of the world: in pralaya Brahman has souls and matter as a subtle body; in creation, as a gross body
present in five forms: para, vyūha, vibhava, antaryāmin, arcā
never apart from Śrī (Lakṣmī)
negations: 'neti neti' (BĀU 2.3.6) denies only the limit 'so much' of what was described, not Brahman's qualities
'nirguṇa' denies the defective qualities born of prakṛti, not the auspicious qualities
Brahman is not touched by the changes and imperfections of its body
views.relation_to_self: The individual self (jīva) is a real, eternal, atomic knower that is a mode (prakāra) and body of Brahman, its servant (śeṣa), wholly dependent (paratantra), never identical with it and never lost in it, even in liberation.
views.relation_to_world: The world is real; it is the body of Brahman, transformed from subtle to gross in creation while Brahman as its self remains unchanged and unaffected.
views.caveat: The tradition affirms one ultimate but rejects any reading of 'one truth' as an attributeless or merely impersonal reality: the one is the personal Nārāyaṇa with Śrī, and souls and world remain real and distinct as his body. It rejects Advaita's identity of self and Brahman and the unreality of the world, and would reject a reconciliation that makes Nārāyaṇa one name among equals for a nameless absolute.

descriptions: pure consciousness, the locus and object of the one beginningless ignorance
the prototype (bimba) of which the jīva is the reflection
negations: as in Advaita generally
views.relation_to_self: The jīva is Brahman's reflection (pratibimba) in avidyā/the inner organ; the reflection is not unreal but identical with the prototype, as a face in a mirror is the face itself.
views.relation_to_world: The world is the transformation (pariṇāma) of avidyā and the apparent transformation (vivarta) of Brahman, which is the locus of avidyā.
views.caveat: Shares Advaita's ultimate; differs from the Bhāmatī line only in the explanatory theory of how the one appears as many. Partisans of the Vivaraṇa hold their theory to be the correct one, not merely a method.

names.name: paśyantī, the supreme station of speech

descriptions: without beginning or end, the principle of the Word, imperishable, appearing as things (VP 1.1)
one, appearing as many through its powers, though not separate from them (VP 1.2)
the single seed of all, existing as enjoyer, enjoyed and enjoyment (VP 1.4)
the Being that all words finally denote (VP 3.1–3.2)
negations: paśyantī is undivided, with all sequence withdrawn (Vṛtti on VP 1.142)
not established by reasoning alone (VP 1.30, 1.34)
views.relation_to_self: Consciousness is of the nature of speech: if the eternal word-nature of awareness departed, light would not illumine (VP 1.124 Iyer); the Word is the inner consciousness of beings.
views.relation_to_world: The world is an appearance (vivarta) of the Word-principle, proceeding through its time-power; the universe evolved first from the Vedic metres (VP 1.1, 1.3, 1.120 Iyer).
views.caveat: The grammarians hold a single ultimate but not a personal Lord. Their identification of the Word (paśyantī) with Brahman is rejected by the Kashmir Śaivas (who place parā vāk above paśyantī), by Buddhist and Jain critics, and by Mīmāṃsā (which denies sphoṭa); whether Bhartṛhari's 'vivarta' means illusory appearance in the later Advaita sense is disputed by scholars.

descriptions: The Vyāsarāja Maṭha holds the Dvaita teaching on the ultimate without variation; see ult:dvaita.
views.relation_to_self: As in ult:dvaita.
views.relation_to_world: As in ult:dvaita.
views.caveat: As in ult:dvaita; the maṭha has no separate doctrine of the ultimate.

descriptions: all-pervading, ever-risen, undivided, independent, spotless; by its will creation and in it dissolution (KJN 3.9–10)
Śiva never without Śakti (KJN 17.8)
all is samarasa, full, the Akulavīra alone (Akulavīra A.41)
negations: not in the supports, aims, channels or breaths; neither near nor far; beyond is and is not (Akulavīra A.15–23, A.34)
views.relation_to_self: The jīva is the supreme Śiva, called jīva while in the body (KJN 6.4–7); the self is its own guru (17.35).
views.relation_to_world: Creation and dissolution occur within the body; the Kula (Śakti's domain) and Akula (Śiva) are inseparable.
views.caveat: The Yoginīkaula's one reality is reached through Kaula practice and secrecy; it declares all other schools bound in conceptual construction (Akulavīra A.7–10), so it would not accept being placed as one view among equals.
